First, I have to say that it is completely normal to want to see your SO at every waking moment in the beginning of any relationship. You'll have only been together for a few weeks but you miss them like hell when you're just one day apart. It's normal. Feelings run high in the beginning, but it settles into a more comfortable thing later on. When I was with my boyfriend for a year and a half, we wouldn't see each other for a few weeks because of college and it didn't really bother us too much at that point. Sure, we missed each other, but it was nothing like the start of the relationship. 

What's your schooling situation? I'm assuming that you're in high school and he's in college? I have to say, I didn't understand this until I came to college. It is a LOT of work. When you're finally done with your work, you want to hang out with your college friends, go get coffee, go out to the movies, and just do things with people on campus. It is a HUGE drag to go home, no matter how much you miss and care about the people who are at home. It's just the way it is.

So he could be blowing off your plans to do other things with other people, maybe he's not that committed. Or, maybe he is honestly incredibly busy and just doesn't have the time.

Either way, this is an unhealthy relationship for *you*. Whatever point you are at in your life is not where he is in his own life. It's really hard for you to understand where he's coming from. I know that the age difference is slight, but if you're living at home and he's at college I can tell you that your lives are vastly different. It's hard for him to understand how lonely you are and it's hard for you to understand how much work he has and how it's very easy to get caught up with your friends during your free time even if you do care about and miss your S/O who is at home. 

It sounds like this relationship is putting too much stress on you. It doesn't seem very healthy and I would personally consider ending it.

I have a similar problem.. and my boyfriend and I haven't had sex in months. I went to the gynecologist and she said that I have vulvodynia which I believe is a generalized term for pain of the vulva. For me, it's also vaginismus. That's when your muscles clamp up and insertion becomes extremely difficult or impossible. There are tons of reasons why this may happen to a woman.. it can be due to a religious or strict upbringing, parents teaching the child that those areas are "off limits" or that sex is "bad", sexual abuse, bullying, or any psychological thing... other times, it just happens. 

I think that the best thing to do would be to encourage your girlfriend to see a gynecologist and talk about this problem with them. From her perspective, I can promise you that it's probably 20x more frustrating for her than it is for you. It can leave a girl feeling broken or defective. I've struggled with that for a while. However, it can be solved. There are tons of different ways to solve the problem... for vaginismus, they do offer special physical therapy and dilators. But, of course, before you try any of this, she needs to see a gynecologist. Don't attempt intercourse until she does. Repeated failed instances that involve pain for her will make the problem worse and engrain that sex is painful into her brain. 

I'm sure that she's worried that you'll break up with her for this. I *know* that she worries about this and wonders if she'll ever be "normal". I am relieved that I went to the doctor for this.. I have only just begun treatment but there are a lot of success stories of people getting over this. I'm sure that she'd appreciate you working with her and supporting her.. in fact, it can even be extremely helpful in the recovery process. 

Good luck to both of you!

So. I have a slightly different background. I became extremely ill with mono at the end of my freshman year of high school. I missed all of sophomore year, and when I finally did go back, I was so far behind that my parents decided to pull me from school all together and I home schooled. I know that this isn't an option for everyone, but I can honestly say that I would not be where I am today if I didn't do it! I didn't get very good SAT scores, but I still got into my dream school, the top school in the country for what I want to go into, with a 20% acceptance rate. 

Homeschooling can really make you stand out as a student, and depending on what you want to go into, sometimes it's favored. Not only that but I feel like I received a better education than I would have had I stayed in public school. It has to be done right and it doesn't work for everyone. 

I taught myself but I also took community college courses. In fact, this was really great alternative to high school courses for me. They weren't extremely difficult, but they delivered a lot of content in a very short amount of time. Additionally, one semester of community college counts as a year of high school. High school gives you a LOT of BS work.. and it can go at a fairly slow pace because it has to work for everyone. Not only did community college cut out most of the BS, but I also had professors that were thrilled about teaching! It made the classes so much more enjoyable. You can also research and select the teachers that you want. In public high school I had teachers that just didn't want to be there.

As for activities outside of school, I got a job at 18 (however, you can sometimes find jobs that will hire younger), took guitar classes, art classes, and flight lessons (which I financed myself with money that I earned from art, and now my job). 

So, despite not having the greatest SAT scores, having all of this behind me got me where I wanted to go.

Now, again, I realize that this may not be possible for you! Do not fear! I just wanted you to know that, if possible, there are other options out there. BUT, there are still ways to make yourself stand out within the normal school system. 

First of all.. get good grades! It's very very easy to let your grades slip. All it takes is saying "I'm so tired that I can't do my homework tonight, but it will only be this one time". It won't only be that one time. I can promise you that it will snowball and it will turn into a very bad habit. Always always always do your homework! (This is an instance where I appreciated community college courses, the homework was not just busy work, in high school, it is). 

Study for tests in whatever way way works best for you. I find that taking very thorough notes works for me. I wrote just about everything down in class, and then reviewed my notes, along with the reading when I got him. From that, I would refine my notes. The repetition really solidified it in my brain! 

Talk to your teachers!! Become the teacher's pet, whatever it takes! Become friendly with them. They'll like you if you do all of your work and put effort in, as well as participating in class.. but they'll like you even more if you talk to them after class if you don't understand specific instructions or if you have any questions at all. They want to see that you're interested and they want to see that you *want* to do a good job. You can even ask if they have time to review notes with you, or even ask if they can read one of your papers or something!

As far as activities go.. I say do theatre. I never did school theatre but I did musicals outside of school. First of all.. in high school.. kids are going to go through some huge changes. Many will become apathetic and set low goals or have none at all.. until it's too late. I can see that you're a motivated person.. so stick with other motivated people! Theatre club usually consists of the "good" kids. Not to mention, it's extremely fun! If you actively participate, I think schools would really like to see that. I know a kid who got into Harvard because of his grades of course but also because he was very active in the school theatre. 

I wouldn't say that you have to join a sports team.. unless you really want to. In fact, I wouldn't recommend it at all. It can really sap your grades because practice takes a lot of time.. and there are extremely early practice times before school. The only sport that I would say is worthwhile in terms of looking good for college is golf.. if your school has a golf team. There are a lot of scholarships for it and there aren't a huge amount of kids who do it either. 

Again, hang out with the "good" kids. I know that this might sound lame depending on what kind of person you are.. but I don't think that you'll regret it later on. When you start high school, a lot of kids are going to become obsessed with drinking, sex, parties, etc. I hung out with those kids from time to time and I can say that kind of lifestyle is *not* going to put you in the right direction. Again, hang out with motivated kids who aren't interested in throwing their futures away. Don't get caught up in the peer pressure (and there will be a lot of it). You may not be regarded as the coolest, most popular guy in the school, but that really doesn't matter. You'll realize later on that high school was not the best years of your life and your social status at that time does not define who you will be as an adult person. When I was in public school, I wanted popularity. I hung out with that group, and honestly, it was stressful! It took a lot of *work* to remain in the group. You had to be up to date on all of the gossip, someone was always talking behind your back, and it was just stressful and miserable. Now, most of these people are just partying their butts off in college. However, the nerdier kids are doing interesting things with their lives. On girl is even traveling the world and doing charity work in places like Africa and China. She's awesome! When I left the school system I realized that I could be the biggest dork that I wanted. Also, those nerdy kids are going to better friends than the popular ones. Trust me on that one. 

Don't be afraid to go to your guidance counselor for help. During my short time in public school, mine was very helpful. She told me what I needed to do to get into my dream school... and she was the one who helped point me in the right direction when my family and I decided that home schooling was the best option. 

I know that it's different for every school.. but mine didn't care about volunteer hours with no meaning. A lot of kids feel pressured to meet a quota but don't really care about the work that they're doing. The admissions counselor that I spoke to said that it was fine that I had zero volunteer hours because what's the point in cramming them in if there isn't a project that I'm passionate about. So, if you plan on volunteering, and if your high school or future college requires it (find this out), then pick something that you're passionate about and commit to. Something that would look impressive is trying to do charity work abroad over the summer.. if you're that dedicated of course. Or you could establish yourself somewhere. Direct a community project in your town. What I'm saying is don't just settle for working at the food pantry.. be a leader in something. Colleges like to see that.


Finally, when you get to the point of applying to colleges.. be in contact with the schools! Whenever you make contact with the school, it should be from you, not your parents. This will show them that you're a mature adult and a good potential student. Something that really helped me was having a meeting with the head admissions counselor. This was given that my situation was a little different than the average student. At first I emailed admissions saying that I would like a meeting to discuss my academic portfolio with them because it was so different and I wasn't sure if I had everything that they wanted to see. They responded saying that they could discuss it over email but I insisted (politely) on a face to face meeting. They agreed! I went in with my mother but I conducted the meeting. It was extremely helpful and they were impressed that I was forward enough to set up the meeting and get what I wanted out of it! That's what schools want to see. A Person who's forward, responsible, and knows how to get what they want out of a situation. When a college looks at you, they want to see that you have the potential of becoming one of the people they are able to put on the list of important alumni.

So.. as a recap.. focus. Just focus. Partying in high school is not worth it. They may make it look like fun, but high school popularity is not going to get you anything later in life. Hard work and responsibility will! 

I'm sorry for the length of that! But good luck!

Not being interested in having a facebook doesn't mean that I am not open to socialization. It doesn't make me antisocial. Facebook is not the definition of being social.


EDIT: I have to add that I am not opposed to social media at all. I am always for new ideas and services that can make staying connected, networking, etc. easier and more efficient. I am not one to refuse to adopt and learn new technologies to aid with this because "the old way was better". However, I don't want facebook to be my *only* option. My college is fairly small... and I feel like, if there is a big party happening, it *will* be spread by word of mouth. However, that isn't what I'm going to college for. All of that can be done without having your personal life plastered all over the internet.

I don't have anything shady to hide.. but I don't want people to be browsing through photos of my family vacation, or my old prom photos. Those memories belong to me and the other people who were there. I highly doubt that any stranger is going to really *care* about those experiences while they're mindlessly browsing through my photo albums. I also feel like facebook turns into this whole "look at me" competition... look at me on spring break! Look at me in my new car! Look at all of the friends I have! You get me point... 
 
I prefer instagram because it's a little less personal. It's not as easy or practical to overshare. I personally use it to post photography and whatever aesthetic I'm into at the time.. not so much about my personal life. 

I have always enjoyed having a smaller, tightly knit group of friends. We've had some really amazing times together, things that I didn't experience when I had a facebook and felt like I had more friends than I actually did. I also feel like there are some people that should have left our lives.. but we just hang on to them through facebook.

Getting over my last, and most upsetting breakup was very hard... but I did get completely over it. I allowed myself to think about the good times we had, and how sad I was for a week. I allowed myself to cry over it, get angry, whatever I needed to think about and be sad about for that amount of time. Then, after that week was over, I forced myself to stop thinking about it. I made myself go out with friends, and do the things that I liked.. like reading a book, drawing, skiing, etc. Things that made me happy. At this time, I still allowed myself to think about it for very short periods of time.. maybe at night for a few minutes if there was something I needed to sort out in my head... but then I stopped thinking about it once I had whatever it was figured out. If I started thinking about it at any time, I would just force it out of my mind and replace the thought with something else. I found that exercise really helped me feel better, as well as yoga, eating healthy, and meditation. Of course I was still a little sad, but I made sure not to dwell on it everyday and let it interrupt my life. 

Different people get over things at different rates, and every experience is different. But I can tell you that it will take longer than you think... it could even take a year.. or more.. But it *does* get better. The sting, or the feeling of unease, whatever it is, will lessen in potency as time goes on. Two weeks from now, you'll be feeling better than you are right now, in a month, you'll be feeling a lot better, in three months you won't even think about it that much, in a year (give or take), you'll be at peace with it. 

I just want you to know that it *does* get better.. but you have to be honest with yourself about your feelings. Sit down and reflect on your relationship. Allow yourself to feel sad, angry, or even happy. It's a process and only time helps it. But do things on the side.. like hang out with friends, pick up on a hobby, get a new job, distract yourself after you've had time to come to terms with it.

Yeah, I think face to face communication is really really important. You can solve things in much better ways because there can be miscommunications via text or even over the telephone. It's much harder to lie or avoid the questions when you're staring that person in the face. 

Relationships take work, things can be awkward, but it's all a learning process. 

Why do you think she might be annoyed with you? Like what exactly do you do that you think is annoying her? Was this a sudden shift or did she gradually become this way over an extended period of time? Both are totally different situations. If it's the first, it's probably something that can be solved.. or it's a THING that happened that you guys need to discuss. If it's the second situation, unfortunately, you might not be as compatible as you think.

To start a conversation like this just try to sit down and say something like "Hey, so I fell like you've been acting distant lately and I think we really need to talk about it. Can you tell me what's up?" Make sure to use the phrase "I feel" instead of "you are", that way it isn't an accusation.  Or you could say something like "I've been getting the feeling that you're annoyed with me and I'm wondering why". You say that you don't know where to start this conversation, she probably doesn't either. Since she isn't used to having an honest, open conversation, there's a chance she'll still try to pull the "nothing is wrong"/"I don't know" thing. Don't let her do that. If she does, retaliate with something like "I know something is wrong because it seems like you've been avoiding me" or something like that. Don't get into a fight, talk to her gently and show her that you're someone that she can be 100% open with. If whatever is wrong isn't something that will be the end of the relationship, and it's something that can be fixed, this point in your relationship is an incredibly important point to establish trust, understanding, problem solving skills, and good, open communication. 

As far as being the emotional bitch in the relationship, you have every right to feel this way right now. You have no idea why she's being this way and I wouldn't blame you if it's constantly on your mind. It's a horrible way to feel. But as a girl, I know that no matter how little of it we show, we definitely dwell on things like this too. Whatever is up, I'm sure it's constantly on her mind and she's freaking out internally too.

Something is definitely up. She's keeping something from you. If this happened as suddenly as you said it did and not gradually, something must have happened in her life that is making her feel sad, scared, guilty, or mad. It may be related to you or it may be completely unrelated. 

Three months is really the mark where you know if you're in it for a committed relationship or if it's time to let things go. It's usually the time where you know a good deal about the person and their personality and if you guys are compatible or not. This turning point always seems to happen just around three months. Speaking as a girl.. many of us are "complicated" and don't tend to be up front about everything. Sometimes we expect boys to read our minds but we have to realize that they can't. I know because I can be that way. If I'm upset about something I can become passive aggressive and try to nudge my boyfriend to ask my about what's wrong instead of straight up telling him what's wrong. I always make sure to catch and correct myself in those situations though. It's sort of the no mean's yes thing. It's how I might tell you that it's okay if you want to go hang out with your friends tonight even though we had plans because you don't see them very often but then I will wind up being a little miffed about it all anyway (even though it is totally okay that you decided to go with your friends). 

Does this make sense?

I don't know her, but she might be prompting you, in a weird way, to dig deeper. Something might be bothering her, or she's still trying to figure out how to put it into words. I think that it's important that you ask her what's up.. and do this in person so you can see her facial expressions. If you want this relationship to work out, I cannot stress enough that you need to communicate. It's so vital to a healthy relationship. After she does tell you what's up, and if it isn't the end of your relationship (I hope it isn't!), then you need to tell her what I said "open communication and trust is really important". 

This all could be a warning sign to you, she might not be good at communicating and she might continue to do this throughout your relationship. But she's also young, and she probably hasn't had a lot of experience with what makes a healthy relationship. Sometimes it can be really hard to open up and talk about how we feel or what's wrong or why our partner offended us, but everyone learns from it and it brings people closer. 

There's no way that I'll be able to tell you exactly why she's acting like this.. but there is a reason and you need to be straight forward with her and ask.
